analytic.title: A Multi-Dimensional Scheduling Scheme for QoS-Aware Real-Time Applications on Heterogeneous Clusters

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Multiple performance guarantees are increasingly needed in QoS-aware real-time applications. Unfortunately, most traditional scheduling algorithms only consider one or two dimensions of them. In this paper, we build a new scheduler model that is suitable for providing multiple services. Based on the scheduler mode, we propose a novel multi-dimensional scheduling scheme MDSS, which tasks timing constraints, QoS, throughput, fairness and load balancing into account. The MDSS includes three steps.

Step 1 is used to provide real-time scheduling and the existing DASAP algorithm is employed in step 1. In step 2, we present a novel algorithm MQFQ that strives to enhance the QoS levels of accepted tasks and makes these tasks have fair QoS services, as well. Another new algorithm ITLB is proposed and used in step 3. The ITLB algorithms is capable of balancing load of nodes and improving throughput of the system. We have performed extensive simulation experiments to compare MDSS scheme with MDSR scheme, DASAP and DALAP algorithms. Experimental results indicate that MDSS improves QoS benefit, has better load balancing and has higher throughput over MDSR, DASAP and DALAP while guaranteeing high schedulability.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Clusters have been increasingly used for scientific and commercial applications for their cost-effective requirement in computing power [1,2]. The nodes usually having their own disks and operating systems in a cluster are interconnected by high-speed networks, and work together to carry out high performance applications. Recently, clusters have also been employed in real-time applications. Examples of real-time applications include aircraft control, signal processing, image processing, etc. Due to the lowcost and high flexibility, clusters are regarded as a fast and cost-effective solution to computationally large and dataintensive problems.

It is well known that scheduling algorithms play an important role to greatly improve the performance of real-time applications running on clusters. However, most existing scheduling algorithms only consider one or two of the dimensions including real-time, QoS, load balancing, fairness and so on. Therefore, these scheduling algorithms are not suitable for some applications with multi-dimensional requirements. For example, in cluster-based real-time signal processing systems, signal processing has the following characteristics: (1) The signal data is able to be divided into independent task blocks to be processed in different nodes. (2) The signal data can be processed using different algorithms. As for decoding block turbo codes, several algorithms can be employed [3,4,5]. Note that, highcomplexity algorithms can guarantee signal processing having higher QoS level at the expense of processing time, but low-complexity algorithms are just the opposite. (3) The conterminous two tasks should be concatenated one by one after processing. So, minimizing the completion time of the task finished latest can improve throughput and decrease delay. (4) Fair QoS are needed to improve the quality of signal processing. Thus, it is significant to provide multidimensional services for these practical applications.

In this paper, we focus on a way of scheduling real-time tasks with multi-dimensional requirements including timing constraints, QoS enhancement, throughput improvement, load balancing and QoS fairness on heterogeneous clusters. We adopt a novel scheduling scheme named MDSS (Multiple Dimensions Scheduling Scheme) with three steps to realize the purpose. (1) Step 1 employs the DASAP algorithm [7] to generally decide the allocation of tasks. (2) Step 2 exploits a novel QoS enhancement algorithm by maximizing QoS benefit, that is Maximal QoS and Fair QoS (MQFQ for short) based on step 1. (3) Step 3 adopts a new algorithm that minimizes standard deviation of nodes' latest finish time to Improve Throughput and Load Balancing (ITLB for short).

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews the related work. In Section 3, we present a realtime scheduler model and a task model. Section 4 proposes the MDSS scheme including two novel algorithms MQFQ and ITLB. Performance evaluation is presented in Section 5. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper.

div.head: Related work
div.p: As we know, optimal scheduling of tasks on a multiprocessor system remains a strong NP-complete problem [8], which motivated the need for heuristic approaches to develop scheduling algorithms. Up to now, many heuristic algorithms have been proposed. Braun et al. evaluated eleven commonly used algorithms OLB, UDA, Fast Greedy, Minmin, Max-min, Greedy, Genetic algorithm (GA), Simulated Annealing (SA), GSA, Tabu and A* [9]. The experimental results show Min-min, GA and A* have good performance. Maheswaran et al. proposed a Sufferage heuristic that has better performance than Min-min [10], etc. Although these algorithms can achieve high throughput and load balancing, they do not take time constraints into consideration.

Many scheduling algorithms have been proposed for real-time systems that can be classified into hard real-time systems [6] and soft real-time systems [11]. In this paper, we consider the system belongs to the latter one. Realtime scheduling algorithms generally fall into two categories: static (off-line) [12] and dynamic (on-line) [7]. Some scheduling algorithms of real-time tasks are preemptive [13,14], whereas our scheduling algorithms are nonpreemptive. Moreover, several algorithms schedule tasks with precedence constraints [12,15]. In contrast, our algorithms like those presented in [16] is independent. Now, more practical applications are applied to heterogeneous clusters because the nodes in clusters generally have different processing powers [7]. Some work has been done to combine real-time computing with heterogeneous systems. Qin and Jiang proposed a real-time scheduling to minimize the reliability cost in heterogeneous systems [7]. Auluck and Agrawal presented a selective task-duplicationbased algorithm to improve the schedulability of real-time heterogeneous multiprocessor systems [17], etc. In our study, the cluster is heterogeneous. All the algorithms above regard higher guarantee ratio as their objective but do not take the other requirements(e.g., QoS requirement, load balancing) into consideration.

The need to support applications with real-time characteristics, such as video-on-demand and speech processing, has motivated research in scheduling algorithms providing quality of service (QoS) guarantees for real-time applications. Abdelzaher et al. presented real-time middleware services for a flight control application by QoS negotiation [6]. etc. The QoS enhancement is only a step in our work and all the tasks on one node have better QoS levels rather than some tasks have highest QoS levels and some tasks have lowest QoS levels. In addition, we adopt a novel approach to balance the load besides enhancing QoS levels, which increases throughput, decreases delay and achieves load balancing.

div.head: Scheduler model
div.p: A scheduler model can be either distributed or centralized [7]. Compared with the distributed scheme, the centralized scheduling model has two attractive features. First, it directly provides the centralized scheduler with faulttolerance using a backup scheduler. Second, implementation is simpler and easier than that of distributed scheduler model. In order to realize our scheduling objectives, we modify the traditional centralized scheduler model and proposed a novel scheduler model illustrated in Figure 1. The scheduler is modeled by a real-time controller, a QoS level controller and a balancing controller. The scheduler and nodes are connected by a high-speed network and each node maintains a local queue in which accepted task are queuing up for execution on the node.

In this study, we build the real-time controller using the DASAP algorithm and other real-time scheduling algorithms can be used, too. The real-time controller determines whether or not a task in schedule queue can be accepted or rejected according to the condition that if the deadline and minimal QoS requirement of a task can be guaranteed. If so, the task will be transferred into the accepted queue; otherwise, the task will be dropped into the rejected queue. The QoS controller aims at maximizing the QoS benefits (Subsection 3.2 will introduce the definition of QoS benefit) of accepted tasks. After being handled by the QoS controller, the balancing controller will adjust the tasks allocation for load balancing and improvement of throughput without changing their QoS levels and missing their deadlines. Finally, these tasks are dispatched to designated nodes for execution.

div.head: Task model
div.p: Let T = {t 1 , t 2 , ..., t n } be a set of independent real-time tasks and N = {n 1 , n 2 , ..., n m } be a set of nodes. The execution time of each task on each node is denoted by a matrix E = (e ij ) n×m , where element e ij denotes the execution time of task t i on node n j . d i is the deadline of task t i . Let EST = (est ij ) n×m be a earliest start time matrix of tasks, where element est ij denotes the earliest start time of task t i on node n j . M is the makespan, M = max 1≤i≤n {f i }, where f i is the finish time of task t i . Let X = (x ij ) n×m be a binary matrix, where element x ij equals 1 if and only if t i has been assigned to n j ; otherwise x ij = 0. CE = (ce ij ) n×m is a binary matrix, where element ce ij equals 1 if and only if the QoS level of t i can be enhanced on n j ; otherwise ce ij = 0. Let QoS levels be a set Q, Q = {q 1 , q 2 , ..., q k }, where q 1 < q 2 < ... < q k .

X i denotes all possible schedules for task t i and x i ∈ X i is a scheduling decision of t i . The QoS level of task t i adopting scheduling x i can be represented by q(x i ). x i is a feasible scheduling if 1) deadline d i can be guaranteed, i.e., f i ≤ d i , and 2) the QoS requirement is satisfied, i.e., q 1 ≤ q(x i ) ≤ q k . div.p: The pseudocode of MQFQ is given in Figure 2. The goal of the MQFQ algorithm is to maximize QoS benefits of tasks while guaranteeing real-time requirements for the tasks running on the same node. To avoid the local extremum problem, we do not let the QoS benefit be monotonic increasing. Thus, the MQFQ algorithm designed to select the task whose QoS level enhancement resulting in maximal new QoS benefit regardless of whether the new QoS benefit is less than the old one or not (see Lines 19-22).
If the QoS level of a task is q k , the task will be deleted from set S (see Lines 7-8), because the QoS level (q k ) cannot be enhanced any more.

Before increasing the QoS level of task t i on node n j , the MQFQ algorithm attempts to verify if the real-time requirement of t i can be met, and the time constraints of tasks whose execution sequence is later than that of t i can be guaranteed (see Line 12). If not, that indicates the tasks QoS level cannot be enhanced any more, so t i is deleted from S (see Line 14). div.head: Performance evaluation
div.p: In this section, we present several groups of experimental results obtained from extensive simulations to evaluate performance of the proposed scheduling scheme. We compare MDSS with DASAP, DALAP algorithms [7] and MDSR scheme including three steps (Step 2 adopts Round-Robin method, step 1 and step 3 are same to those of MDSS). To make the comparisons fair, we slightly modify the DASAP and DALAP in such a way that they arbitrarily pick a security level within the QoS range of tasks.
In our experiments, we evaluate the performance in the following metrics:
(1) Guarantee Ratio (GR);
(2) QoS Benefit Average (QBA) on all nodes;
(3) QoS Level Average (QLA); (4) QoS Level Standard Deviation (QLSD);
(5) Makespan (MS); (6) Finish Time Standard Deviation (FTSD) of nodes.

div.head: Simulation method and parameters
div.p: The simulation method is as follows:

(1) To present the node heterogeneity, we use p j a positive real number to represent the processing power of node n j . The powerAverage and powerSpan denote the average processing power of all nodes and variable scope taking powerAverage as center, respectively. p j is uniformly distributed between powerAverage -powerSpan and powerAverage + powerSpan.

(2) We employ h i -a positive real number to denotes the hardness of task t i . Parameters hardnessAverage and hardnessSpan denote the average hardness of all tasks and variable scope taking hardnessAverage as center, respectively. The value of h i is uniformly chosen between hardnessAverage -hardnessSpan and hardnessAverage + hardnessSpan.

(3) The execution time matrix E = (e ij ) n×m in our study belongs to the Consistent matrix [10]. e ij = (1 + q(x i )/10) × baseT ime × (h i /p j ), (0 ≤ q(x i ) ≤ 9). Parameter baseT ime is a random positive real number and q(x i ) is a positive integer.

(4) The deadline d i of task t i is calculated as follows: d i = a i +max{e ij }+baseDeadline, where a i is the arrival time. max{e ij } is the maximal execution time of t i on all nodes. baseDeadline is a random positive real number and determines that tasks have loose deadlines or not.
(5) The ready time r i is chosen between 0 and readyT ime. Parameter readyT ime is a random positive real number.
Table 1 gives the simulation parameters and their values.

div.head: Performance impact of node number
div.p: In this subsection, we observe the performance comparisons on the impact of node number. Figure 4(a) shows that the MDSS and MDSR have the identical guarantee ratio (GR) and improve it over DASAP and DALAP by up to 16.79 % and 13.54% on average, respectively. This result can be attributed to the fact that the MDSS and MDSR both adopt DASAP algorithm in step 1 and set the QoS levels of all tasks to the lowest value. However, the DASAP randomly picks up QoS levels for tasks. Therefore, the MDSS and MDSR outperform DASAP in this aspect. In addition, the MDSS and MDSR do not add and drop any task in step 2 and step 3, so they are always have the same GR. With the increase of node number, more nodes can process more tasks within the time constraints, thus the GR of all grows.

Figure 4(b)-(d) show that the QBA, QLA and QLSD of DASAP and DALAP approach constant values, whereas the same aspects of MDSS and MDSR are inclined to our objectives (high QoS levels average and low difference of QoS levels), which results from the DASAP and DALAP do not adopt the QoS enhancement mechanism. Figure 4(b) shows that the QBA of MDSS maintains a small constant value 1 when node number is less than 25, which can be explained that if there are less nodes in the system, the MDSS regards the high GR as its main objective. So in Figure 4(c)-(d), the MDSS has slight improvement of QLA and higher QLSD when node number is less than 25. When the node number is more than 25, the GR of MDSS is greatly improved because the constraints become loose (Property 1), the QBA and QLA of MDSS increase and QLSD decreases correspondingly. That is because the MDSS is capable of employing slack times to improve the QoS levels of the accepted tasks. When the node number increases more than 25, all tasks can be accepted and the constraints are much looser, so the QoS levels of all tasks can achieve the highest level, the QBAs have the biggest value and the QLSDs equal zero. For the MDSR, because it employs Round-Robin method in step 2, so the QLSD of MDSR basically keep invariable. The QBA and QLA change of MDSR have the same reason as MDSS.

Figure 4(e) shows that the makespans of MDSS and MDSR decrease when the node number increases. That is because they exploit the load balancing method. Figure 4(f) illustrates that with the increase of node number, the MDSS, MDSR and DASAP all have better load balancing, but DALAP allocates a task to the node on which it has the latest start time, which makes the load balancing very worse.

div.head: Performance impact of power span
div.p: Here, we examine how the power span that decides the heterogeneity of nodes affects the performance of MDSS, MDSR, DASAP and DALAP. The experimental results are illustrated in Figure 5.

From Fig. 5(b)-(d), we can see that QBA, QLA and QLSD of MDSS improve with the increase of node heterogeneity because the accepted task number slightly decreases with the increase of node heterogeneity. Although the node heterogeneity is changed, the whole processing power of nodes is changeless in our experiments, so the accepted tasks have more slack time to be used by MDSS to enhance the QoS levels.

Figure 5(e) shows that the makespan of MDSS slightly decreases with the interpretation that the accepted task number decreases. However, the makespan of DALAP still keep invariable despite less accepted tasks, which reveals that DALAP has poor flexibility. Figure 5(f) plots the MDSS, MDSR and DASAP can guarantee the system has better load balancing regardless of the changed node heterogeneity, but the DALAP shows the worse load balancing with the increase of node heterogeneity.

All the experiments in this group reflect that the node heterogeneity have slightly effect on the MDSS. Though the GR decreases a little, other aspects are improved and the load is still balanceable. Therefore, the MDSS has perfect adaptivity.

div.head: Performance impact of base deadline
div.p: In this subsection, we want to see when the tasks have loose time, how the slack time is used.

Figure 6(a) shows when the deadlines become loose, the MDSS, MDSR, DASAP and DALAP all boost up GR. This is because the time constraints are not rigid as before. Meanwhile, the MDSS and MDSR have higher GRs than DASAP and DALAP, which are as explained in group one experiment. Though tasks have more slack time when their deadlines become loose, Figure 6(b)-(d) show that the DASAP and DALAP do not improve QoS levels. Because they do not adopt any QoS enhancement mechanism, so the slack time of accepted tasks are wasted. However, MDSR makes full use of the slack time to enhance QoS benefit within the time constraints, thus, we can see from Figure 6(b)-(d) that the QBA and QLA increase and the QLSD decreases with the increase of base deadline.

Figure 6(e) shows that the makespans of all increase when base deadline is less than 50 for the more accepted tasks. However, the makespan of MDSS basically keeps a constant value and noticeably outperforms than others when the base deadline is more than 50. This is because we use load balancing algorithm in step 3 of MDSS, which make the system have higher throughput.

Figure 6(f) reveals that with the increase of base deadline, the MDSS, MDSR and DASAP all have better load balancing, but the DALAP allocates more tasks to some nodes and others nodes have fewer tasks, which makes the system's load unbalanced.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we have proposed a scheduler model which is efficient to provide multiple performance guarantees for QoS-aware real-time applications running on heterogeneous clusters. According to the scheduler model, a novel scheduling scheme named MDSS is investigated in this paper. The MDSS scheme adopts three steps. In Step 1, any existing real-time scheduling algorithm can be used to satisfy the timing constraint, which greatly improves the flexibility and expansibility of the system. In this paper, we use DASAP algorithm in Step 1. Two novel heuristic algorithms called MQFQ and ITLB are proposed and used in Step 2 and Step 3, respectively. The MQFQ is a fair algorithm that makes all the tasks in one node have higher QoS levels and the difference of QoS levels is minimal on the basis of Step 1. In addition, this QoS level enhancement method will not produce local extremum. The ITLB algorithm makes the system achieve load balancing by minimizing the standard deviation of nodes finish time. We compare the MDSS scheme with DASAP, DALAP algorithms and MDSR scheme and the experimental results show that the MDSS outperforms others with respect to guarantee ratio, QoS benefit, throughput and load balancing.
